content: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. {{v:2}} The same was in the beginning with God. {{v:3}} All things were made through him. Without him, nothing was made that has been made. {{v:4}} In him was life, and the life was the light of men. {{v:5}} The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.

facets.evidence: The passage states 'the Word was with God' (distinction) and 'the Word was God' (divinity), and the step to Nicene consubstantiality is the Church's long-settled reading of this text.
facets.text: The Prologue teaches that the Word (the Son) is eternal and truly divine, existing before creation, yet personally distinct from the Father: he 'was with God' and 'was God.' This grounds the Church's Trinitarian and Nicene confession of the Son as consubstantial with the Father.
facets.question: How does the opening of John's Gospel show that the Son is both God and distinct from the Father?

facets.evidence: John's opening 'In the beginning' directly echoes Genesis 1:1, and the tradition has long read this as a deliberate Christological reframing of creation through the Word.
facets.text: By echoing Genesis 1:1, John reveals that the eternal Word is the agent through whom all things were made; nothing that exists came to be apart from him. Creation itself is Christological, spoken into being through the Son.
facets.question: What is the connection between John's Prologue and the Genesis creation story?

facets.evidence: The passage states 'in him was life, and the life was the light of men' but the identification of this life and light with Christ's later self-declarations requires connecting this verse to later Johannine texts.
facets.text: The Word possesses life in himself and is the source of light for humanity; this life and light are not abstract gifts but the person of Christ, who later declares himself the light of the world and the life.
facets.question: What does it mean that the Word is the life and light of humankind?

facets.evidence: The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn't overcome it.
facets.text: The light of the Word shines continually in the darkness of sin and unbelief, and the darkness can neither extinguish nor comprehend it. This affirms the enduring victory of divine light over the forces opposed to God.
facets.question: Why does John say the darkness has not overcome the light?

merged.annotation:
SUMMARY: The Prologue of John's Gospel (John 1:1–5) establishes the eternal divinity and personal distinction of the Word (Logos), his role as agent of creation, and his identity as the life and light of humanity that no darkness can overcome — foundational texts for Trinitarian theology, Christology, and the theology of creation.

[doctrinal/scriptural | settled]: The Logos existed before all creation, was personally present with the Father ("with God"), and was himself fully divine ("was God") — the scriptural basis for the Nicene confession of the Son as consubstantial with the Father while remaining a distinct divine Person within the Trinity.

[typological/scriptural | settled]: John's deliberate echo of Genesis 1:1 ("in the beginning") identifies the pre-existent Son as the mediator of all creation; every creature owes its existence to the Word, making the doctrine of creation inherently Christological in character.

[doctrinal/scriptural | inferential]: The Word is not merely a channel of life and illumination but their very source — a truth that anticipates Christ's own declarations as the light of the world and the resurrection and the life, suggesting that these gifts are inseparable from his person.

[doctrinal/devotional | explicit]: The light of the Logos shines without interruption into the realm of sin and unbelief, and the powers of darkness have neither extinguished nor comprehended it — an affirmation of the definitive, ongoing victory of divine light over every force opposed to God.
